newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: MCI tool under fire but RBNZ says its working well.
newsitem.headline: MCI tool under fire but RBNZ says its working well.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's conduct of monetary policy using an index tool is under fire, but the bank said on Friday it has worked admirably.
The new Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), launched in June, measures conditions and ensures the bank stays on track to meet its government-imposed 0-3 percent inflation target.
But its critics, and there are many, say the index has caused a perverse situation of raising short term interest rates in a slowing economy, which may turn a forecast growth spurt into a recession.
UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said the recent rise in short-term and mortgage rates will depress consumer spending, highlighting the MCI-induced problems.

"I feel that part of the problem with the Monetary Conditions Index is that at this weaker stage of the economic cycle it has too much of an automatic reaction in terms of short term interest rates moving up when the currency comes under downward pressure," Roberts said.
The index comprises the 90-day bank bill rate and the NZ dollar Trade-Weighted Index and is constructed so that a two percent TWI fall can be offset by a one percent rise in bills.
Since implementation of the MCI in June, the TWI has fallen five percent which, because of the two-for-one ratio, has resulted in bank bills rising steeply to compensate.
But Roberts and others say there is no sign of the lower currency feeding inflation because of sluggish activity.
"I believe the Monetary Conditions Index is far too sensitive in terms of forcing up short term interest rates in these circumstances.
"The net result of this is that domestic demand in New Zealand is likely to remain very, very restrained."
BNZ Treasury Economist Peter Jolly sternly criticises both the MCI concept and the implementation.
He argues that although the MCI has fallen over 200 points since March to 715, conditions have actually almost tightened.
"It's perverse. It's questionable if conditions have eased at all."
He says the RBNZ's rosy growth forecast are predicated on a domestic recovery and higher interest rates will inhibit that.
"And the dollar hasn't fallen far enough to suggest an export-led recovery. For the near term, the changes in conditions are negative for growth."
Jolly attacks the bank's quarterly forecasting of the MCI and its defence of "desired" MCI levels and the "comfort zone".

In June the bank forecast the MCI should average 825 over the September quarter and initially it would allow a 50 point band either side. But it also said that as the quarter proceeded it would be more tolerant as more economic data came to hand.
RB Deputy Governor Murray Sherwin, in reply to an article by Jolly, said on Friday that far from abandoning the MCI as some have suggested, "the MCI has done its job admirably".
It was wrong to blame the MCI for volatility in the exchange or interest rates where in fact much of that turbulance had come from global markets, he argued.
Sherwin said markets had adjusted for a substantial move in the currency without the bank having to comment or intervene.
But Jolly predicts the MCI system will end in tears.
"The bank will have to move to an an implementation model similar to every other central bank -- they will have to move to an official cash rate system."
The RB this year looked at such a system earlier this year and rejected it.
